morning-rules.docTitle: Do Morning Routines Reduce Your Afternoon Energy Crash?
morning-rules.docSubtitle: Evidence Summary for a 6-Week Personal Exploration
morning-rules.summaryShort: The post-lunch dip is partly biological, but its severity is strongly modulated by morning behaviour. Four interventions have meaningful evidence: early sunlight (strong), morning movement (moderate–strong), delayed caffeine (moderate), and morning meditation (moderate).
morning-rules.intro: The post-lunch dip (roughly 1–3pm) is partly biological — a natural circadian trough in alertness — but its severity is strongly modulated by morning behaviour. Four morning interventions have meaningful evidence behind them.

interventions.title: 1. Early Sunlight Exposure
interventions.mechanism: Morning light hitting the retina triggers the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) to release a cortisol pulse and suppress melatonin, anchoring your 24-hour clock. A well-anchored clock produces a sharper, more defined alertness curve — meaning the afternoon trough is shallower and briefer.
interventions.evidence: A landmark study by Wright et al. (2013) showed that just one week of natural light exposure reset circadian timing by ~2 hours and dramatically reduced social jetlag. Leocadio-Miguel et al. (2017) found that outdoor light exposure in the morning was the strongest environmental predictor of circadian alignment across a large population sample.
interventions.practical: 10–30 minutes of outdoor light within 30–60 minutes of waking appears sufficient on bright days; overcast days require longer exposure.

sources.label: Wright KP et al. (2013). Entrainment of the Human Circadian Clock to the Natural Light-Dark Cycle. Current Biology.
Leocadio-Miguel MA et al. (2017). Daytime light exposure as a zeitgeber. Scientific Reports.

interventions.title: 2. Morning Stretching / Movement
interventions.mechanism: Light-to-moderate morning movement elevates core body temperature and amplifies the cortisol awakening response (CAR) — a natural cortisol surge in the first 30–45 minutes post-waking. A stronger CAR is associated with better sustained cognitive performance and reduced fatigue across the day.
interventions.evidence: Clow et al. (2010) comprehensively reviewed the CAR and established its role as a preparatory stress-inoculation response — people with blunted CARs show worse sustained attention. Separate work by Myllymäki et al. found that morning exercise had significantly less disruption to subsequent sleep architecture than evening exercise, suggesting it works with the body’s clock rather than against it.

sources.label: Clow A et al. (2010). The cortisol awakening response: methodological issues and significance. Stress.
Myllymäki T et al. (2011). Effects of vigorous late-night exercise on sleep quality. Journal of Sleep Research.

interventions.title: 3. Caffeine Offsetting (Delaying First Coffee 90–120 Minutes Post-Waking)
interventions.mechanism: Adenosine — the molecule that drives sleepiness — is cleared during sleep but begins rebuilding immediately on waking. If you consume caffeine before adenosine has rebuilt to a meaningful level, you block receptors that aren’t yet occupied, producing a weaker effect and a sharper rebound crash in the afternoon. Waiting 90–120 minutes allows adenosine to partially accumulate, making caffeine more effective and its wear-off more gradual.
interventions.evidence: Landolt (2008) established the adenosine–caffeine interaction mechanism in detail. The specific timing application draws on pharmacokinetic models of adenosine receptor occupancy and has been synthesised by researchers including Huberman (Stanford) in applied neuroscience contexts, though direct RCT evidence on the 90-minute offset is limited — this remains the most hypothesis-driven of the four interventions.

sources.label: Landolt HP (2008). Sleep homeostasis: a role for adenosine in humans? Biochemical Pharmacology.
Nehlig A (2010). Is caffeine a cognitive enhancer? Journal of Alzheimer’s Disease.

interventions.title: 4. Morning Meditation
interventions.mechanism: A short morning meditation practice (10–20 minutes) reduces baseline cortisol reactivity across the day and improves heart rate variability (HRV) — a marker of autonomic nervous system regulation. Higher HRV is consistently associated with better sustained attention and lower mental fatigue in the afternoon hours.
interventions.evidence: Turakitwanakan et al. (2013) found that mindfulness meditation significantly reduced salivary cortisol. A meta-analysis by Pascoe et al. (2017) across 45 studies confirmed that meditation reliably reduces cortisol, with morning practice timing showing particular effect on diurnal cortisol slope — the rate at which cortisol naturally declines across the day, which directly shapes afternoon alertness.

sources.label: Turakitwanakan W et al. (2013). Effects of mindfulness meditation on serum cortisol. Journal of the Medical Association of Thailand.
Pascoe MC et al. (2017). Mindfulness mediates the physiological markers of stress. Journal of Psychiatric Research.

morning-rules.note: These four behaviours are not mutually exclusive — circadian, hormonal, and autonomic pathways interact. A 6-week exploration isolating each variable for 1–2 weeks before combining them will give cleaner signal on which has the most impact for you individually.

relaxation.docTitle: Do Relaxation Practices Improve My Composure?
relaxation.docSubtitle: Evidence Summary for a 6-Week Personal Exploration
relaxation.summaryShort: Composure reflects autonomic balance between stress and recovery. Four practices have strong evidence: vagal breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, short nature walks, and meditation or visualisation — each acting through distinct parasympathetic pathways.
relaxation.intro: Composure is governed by the balance between the sympathetic (fight-or-flight) and parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) branches of the autonomic nervous system. Chronic stress tilts this balance toward sympathetic dominance, elevating cortisol, reducing HRV, and sensitising the amygdala. The four practices below engage the parasympathetic system through distinct but complementary mechanisms.

interventions.title: 1. Vagal Breathing
interventions.mechanism: Slow breathing at 4–6 breaths per minute activates the vagus nerve via an extended exhale, producing rapid increases in HRV and suppressing amygdala and cortisol activity within minutes.
interventions.evidence: Zaccaro et al. (2018) reviewed 15 controlled studies and found that slow breathing consistently reduced anxiety and cortisol with effects measurable in a single 5-minute session. Extended-exhale protocols showed larger effect sizes than equal inhale-exhale ratios. Brown and Gerbarg (2005) found durable HRV improvements and clinical reductions in anxiety after 4 weeks of regular practice.

sources.label: Zaccaro A et al. (2018). How Breath-Control Can Change Your Life. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience.
Brown RP & Gerbarg PL. (2005). Sudarshan Kriya Yogic Breathing in the Treatment of Stress and Anxiety. Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine.

interventions.title: 2. Progressive Muscle Relaxation (PMR)
interventions.mechanism: Chronic stress produces persistent muscular tension that feeds back to the brain, sustaining the threat response. PMR systematically tenses and releases muscle groups, generating a pronounced relaxation rebound that signals physical safety to the nervous system via the vagus nerve.
interventions.evidence: Manzoni et al. (2008) meta-analysed 27 controlled studies and found PMR produced large, consistent reductions in both state and trait anxiety (Cohen's d = 0.57), building over 4–8 weeks. Conrad and Roth (2007) found physiological arousal markers (heart rate, skin conductance) reduced to levels comparable to CBT outcomes for mild-to-moderate anxiety.

sources.label: Manzoni GM et al. (2008). Relaxation training for anxiety: a ten-years systematic review with meta-analysis. BMC Psychiatry.
Conrad A & Roth WT. (2007). Muscle relaxation therapy for anxiety disorders. Journal of Anxiety Disorders.

interventions.title: 3. Short Nature Walks
interventions.mechanism: Natural environments engage involuntary effortless attention, allowing directed attention networks to recover (Attention Restoration Theory). Natural visual stimuli simultaneously activate the parasympathetic system and suppress cortisol through evolutionary responses to safe, resource-rich environments (Stress Recovery Theory).
interventions.evidence: Bratman et al. (2015) showed in PNAS that a 90-minute nature walk significantly reduced both rumination and subgenual prefrontal cortex activity — the brain region linked to repetitive negative thought — with no effect seen in urban walkers. Hunter et al. (2019) found that just 20–30 minutes in a natural setting produced significant salivary cortisol reductions, with effects plateauing beyond 30 minutes, suggesting short daily exposures are as effective as longer ones.

sources.label: Bratman GN et al. (2015). Nature experience reduces rumination and subgenual prefrontal cortex activation. PNAS.
Hunter MR et al. (2019). Urban nature experiences reduce stress based on salivary biomarkers. Frontiers in Psychology.

interventions.title: 4. Meditation and Visualisation
interventions.mechanism: Mindfulness meditation strengthens prefrontal cortex regulation of the amygdala, reducing emotional reactivity. With regular practice, structural brain changes occur — amygdala grey matter density decreases and prefrontal cortex thickness increases. Guided visualisation activates the parasympathetic system through mental simulation of safe environments.
interventions.evidence: Hofmann et al. (2010) meta-analysed 39 studies and found mindfulness-based interventions produced large reductions in anxiety (Hedges' g = 0.63) with effects maintained at follow-up, indicating durable trait-level change. Lazar et al. (2005) provided neuroimaging evidence of greater cortical thickness in meditators. Khoury et al. (2015), focusing specifically on healthy non-clinical individuals, found significant stress, anxiety, and rumination reductions with an average of 8 weeks of practice.

sources.label: Hofmann SG et al. (2010). The Effect of Mindfulness-Based Therapy on Anxiety and Depression: A Meta-Analytic Review. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology.
Lazar SW et al. (2005). Meditation experience is associated with increased cortical thickness. NeuroReport.
Khoury B et al. (2015). Mindfulness-based stress reduction for healthy individuals: A meta-analysis. Journal of Psychosomatic Research.

summaryTable.effect: Rapid stress reduction; acute composure within days
Reduced trait anxiety; builds over 4–8 weeks
Lower rumination; measurable in single sessions
Durable stress reactivity reduction; structural brain change

practicalNotes: Speed of effect: breathing and nature walks improve composure within a single session; PMR builds over 2–3 weeks; meditation requires 4+ weeks for durable trait-level change.
Efficient pairing: a nature walk with slow breathing combines cortisol-reduction and vagal pathways simultaneously — an effective lunchtime or morning slot.
Objective tracking: resting HRV (via Apple Watch, Garmin, Oura, or Whoop) is the most reliable physiological signal that these practices are working — more consistent than mood self-report alone.
Consistency over intensity: 10 minutes of daily practice outperforms 60-minute sessions twice a week for all four interventions.
relaxation.note: Composure is both a state (how calm you feel right now) and a trait (how readily you return to calm after disruption). Breathing and nature walks shift state rapidly; PMR and meditation shift trait over time. Testing each in rotating 10-day blocks before combining will identify which pathway has the greatest personal leverage.

upf-mood.docTitle: Does Reduction of Ultra-Processed Food Improve My Mood?
upf-mood.docSubtitle: Evidence Summary for a 6-Week Personal Exploration
upf-mood.summaryShort: UPFs now account for much of daily intake in the UK and US. Mood links to four modifiable pathways: gut-brain signalling, neuroinflammation, blood glucose stability, and nutrient displacement — each supported by growing clinical evidence.
upf-mood.intro: Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) — defined by the NOVA classification as industrially formulated products containing substances not used in home cooking (e.g. emulsifiers, artificial flavours, hydrogenated oils, high-fructose corn syrup) — now account for 50–60% of daily caloric intake in the UK and US. The link between UPF consumption and mood is increasingly well-supported and operates through four distinct biological pathways, each of which is meaningfully modifiable within a 6-week dietary shift.

interventions.title: 1. Gut-Brain Axis and Microbiome Disruption
interventions.mechanism: Approximately 90–95% of the body's serotonin is synthesised in the gut by enterochromaffin cells, with production directly influenced by the gut microbiome. UPFs disrupt microbial diversity through their low fibre content, high refined sugar load, and chemical additives — particularly emulsifiers such as carboxymethylcellulose and polysorbate-80, which have been shown to degrade the gut mucus layer and alter microbial composition. A disrupted microbiome produces less serotonin, more inflammatory metabolites, and reduced levels of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that are critical for gut-brain signalling via the vagus nerve.
interventions.evidence: Cryan and Dinan (2012) established the foundational framework for the gut-brain axis in Nature Reviews Neuroscience, demonstrating that gut microbial composition directly influences anxiety and depressive-like behaviours through multiple neurochemical pathways. Sonnenburg and Sonnenburg (2019) and subsequent large-scale dietary intervention studies have shown that high-fibre, low-UPF diets significantly increase microbial diversity within 2–4 weeks. Lassale et al. (2019), in a meta-analysis of 41 studies in Molecular Psychiatry, found that dietary patterns rich in whole foods were associated with a 24–35% lower risk of depression, with gut microbiome modulation identified as a primary mediating pathway.
interventions.practical: Replacing UPFs with whole plant foods — particularly diverse vegetables, legumes, and fermented foods — directly feeds beneficial bacteria (especially Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species) associated with improved mood and reduced anxiety.

sources.label: Cryan JF & Dinan TG. (2012). Mind-altering microorganisms: the impact of the gut microbiota on brain and behaviour. Nature Reviews Neuroscience.
Lassale C et al. (2019). Healthy dietary indices and risk of depressive outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies. Molecular Psychiatry.

interventions.title: 2. Neuroinflammation
interventions.mechanism: UPFs promote chronic low-grade systemic inflammation through multiple routes: high omega-6 to omega-3 ratios (promoting pro-inflammatory eicosanoids), advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) from high-heat processing, and emulsifiers that increase intestinal permeability ('leaky gut'), allowing lipopolysaccharide (LPS) — a bacterial endotoxin — to enter systemic circulation. Elevated LPS triggers microglial activation in the brain, producing neuroinflammation. Neuroinflammation is now a well-established feature of major depressive disorder and is directly associated with anhedonia, fatigue, and impaired emotional regulation.
interventions.evidence: Jacka et al. (2017) published the landmark SMILES trial in BMC Medicine — the first randomised controlled trial to test a dietary intervention for depression. Participants following a whole-food Mediterranean-style diet (directly replacing UPF-heavy eating patterns) showed significantly greater reductions in depression scores (on the MADRS scale) compared to social support controls, with 32% achieving remission vs. 8% in the control group. The authors identified reduced inflammatory biomarkers as a key mediating mechanism. Gomez-Donoso et al. (2020), using the SUN cohort (n > 14,000), found that high UPF consumption was associated with a 33% increased risk of incident depression over a median 10-year follow-up.

sources.label: Jacka FN et al. (2017). A randomised controlled trial of dietary improvement for adults with major depression (the 'SMILES' trial). BMC Medicine.
Gomez-Donoso C et al. (2020). Ultra-processed food consumption and the incidence of depression in a Mediterranean cohort: the SUN Project. European Journal of Nutrition.

interventions.title: 3. Blood Glucose Dysregulation and Mood Volatility
interventions.mechanism: UPFs are predominantly composed of rapidly digested refined carbohydrates and added sugars that produce sharp postprandial blood glucose spikes. These spikes trigger a disproportionate insulin response, causing blood glucose to fall below fasting levels (reactive hypoglycaemia). Low blood glucose is directly experienced as irritability, anxiety, low motivation, and emotional reactivity — symptoms that are often misattributed to mood disorders rather than nutritional patterns. Over time, chronic glycaemic variability also impairs hippocampal function, a brain region critical for emotional regulation and stress resilience.
interventions.evidence: Knüppel et al. (2017) analysed data from over 23,000 participants in the UK Biobank and found that high sugar intake — the defining feature of most UPFs — was associated with significantly higher rates of common mental disorders, depression, and anxiety, with the association strongest in men and independent of other dietary factors. A controlled trial by Breymeyer et al. (2016) demonstrated that a high-glycaemic diet produced measurably worse mood, fatigue, and cognitive performance compared to a low-glycaemic diet within just 4 days, suggesting the mood effects of blood glucose dysregulation are rapid and reversible.

sources.label: Knüppel A et al. (2017). Sugar intake from sweet food and beverages, common mental disorder and depression: prospective findings from the Whitehall II study. Scientific Reports.
Breymeyer KL et al. (2016). Subjective mood and energy levels of healthy weight and overweight/obese healthy adults on high- and low-glycemic load experimental diets. Appetite.

interventions.title: 4. Nutrient Displacement and Neurotransmitter Synthesis
interventions.mechanism: UPFs are calorically dense but micronutrient-poor. Diets high in UPFs systematically crowd out the whole foods that supply nutrients essential for neurotransmitter synthesis and mood regulation: omega-3 fatty acids (EPA/DHA) required for serotonin receptor function and anti-inflammatory signalling; B vitamins (B6, B9, B12) required for methylation pathways and dopamine/serotonin synthesis; zinc and magnesium, which modulate NMDA glutamate receptors implicated in depression; and tryptophan (the dietary precursor to serotonin), which competes poorly for brain uptake when displaced by other amino acids from high-protein processed foods.
interventions.evidence: Opie et al. (2015) conducted a systematic review in Nutritional Neuroscience specifically examining the nutrient composition of pro-mood dietary patterns and found that the largest effect sizes were associated with omega-3 fatty acids, B vitamins, and zinc — all of which are consistently lower in UPF-heavy diets. Parletta et al. (2019) conducted an RCT (the HELFIMED trial) in which omega-3 supplementation combined with a Mediterranean diet improved depression scores significantly over 6 months, with nutrient restoration identified as the primary driver. Importantly, the dietary shift in their study involved explicitly replacing UPFs with whole foods rather than simply adding supplements.

sources.label: Opie RS et al. (2015). Dietary recommendations for the prevention of depression. Nutritional Neuroscience.
Parletta N et al. (2019). A Mediterranean-style dietary intervention supplemented with fish oil improves diet quality and mental health in people with depression. Nutritional Neuroscience.

summaryTable.mechanism: Deficits in omega-3, B vits, zinc, Mg

practicalNotes: Defining UPFs: use the NOVA classification as your guide — Group 4 foods include packaged snacks, soft drinks, flavoured yoghurts, processed meats, instant noodles, and most branded breakfast cereals.
Replacement matters as much as removal: the mood benefit comes largely from what replaces UPFs — oily fish, leafy greens, legumes, nuts, and fermented foods — not simply from eating less of them.

Timeline: gut microbiome changes are detectable within 2 weeks of dietary change; neuroinflammation markers typically reduce within 4–6 weeks; neurotransmitter synthesis improvements may take the full 6 weeks to manifest as noticeable mood changes.

Mood tracking: use a validated brief scale (e.g. the PHQ-2, WEMWBS, or a simple 1–10 daily mood + energy log) at consistent times — ideally mid-morning and early evening — to capture both baseline and diurnal mood patterns.
upf-mood.note: The dietary psychiatry field is still maturing, but the evidence base is now sufficient that the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists (2015) and the International Society for Nutritional Psychiatry Research formally recognise diet as a modifiable risk factor for depression. The SMILES trial remains the strongest single piece of evidence: a true RCT showing clinically significant mood improvement from a whole-food diet shift within 12 weeks — with effects visible from week 4 onwards.

screen-sleep.docTitle: Does Moderation of Screen Exposure Improve My Sleep Quality?
screen-sleep.docSubtitle: Evidence Summary for a 6-Week Personal Exploration
screen-sleep.summaryShort: Evening screens affect sleep through four compounding pathways — blue-light melatonin suppression, cognitive arousal, circadian delay, and sleep architecture disruption. Evidence is strongest for a 60–90 minute pre-bed screen-free window.
screen-sleep.intro: The relationship between evening screen use and poor sleep is one of the most replicated findings in modern sleep science. Screens affect sleep through four distinct but compounding pathways — not simply because of blue light, but also through cognitive arousal, circadian disruption, and the displacement of sleep-promoting behaviours. The evidence is particularly strong for the 60–90 minutes immediately before bed.

interventions.title: 1. Blue Light and Melatonin Suppression
interventions.mechanism: Screens emit short-wavelength blue light (peak ~480nm) which is detected by intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) containing melanopsin. These cells are disproportionately sensitive to blue light and directly signal the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) to suppress melatonin production from the pineal gland. Melatonin is the primary hormonal signal that initiates the body's transition to sleep — its suppression delays sleep onset, reduces total sleep time, and impairs the depth of early sleep cycles.
interventions.evidence: Chang et al. (2015) conducted a controlled crossover study at Harvard in which participants read on light-emitting devices vs. printed books for 4 hours before bed over 5 nights. Screen readers showed significantly suppressed melatonin levels (by up to 55%), took longer to fall asleep, experienced less REM sleep, and reported lower morning alertness — effects that persisted even after sleeping a full night. Cajochen et al. (2011) demonstrated that even 2 hours of LED screen exposure in the evening measurably delayed melatonin onset and reduced subjective sleepiness.
interventions.practical: Most research points to the 60–90 minutes before intended sleep as the critical window. Even low-brightness screen use during this period can suppress melatonin meaningfully.

sources.label: Chang AM et al. (2015). Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness. PNAS.
Cajochen C et al. (2011). Evening exposure to a light-emitting diodes (LED)-backlit computer screen affects circadian physiology and cognitive performance. Journal of Applied Physiology.

interventions.title: 2. Cognitive and Emotional Arousal from Content
interventions.mechanism: Sleep onset requires a reduction in cortical arousal — the brain must transition from high-frequency beta and gamma activity to lower-frequency alpha and theta waves. Engaging screen content (news feeds, social media, video, messaging) maintains or increases cognitive arousal by triggering dopamine-mediated engagement loops, emotional responses, and unresolved social or informational processing. This keeps the prefrontal cortex and limbic system active at precisely the time they need to wind down.
interventions.evidence: Exelmans and Van den Bulck (2015) surveyed over 800 adults and found that bedtime mobile phone use — specifically interactive, content-driven use — was independently associated with shorter sleep duration, poorer sleep quality, and greater daytime fatigue, even after controlling for total screen time. The content type mattered: passive viewing had weaker effects than interactive social media and messaging. Hale and Guan (2015) conducted a systematic review of 67 studies and found consistent associations between evening screen use and reduced sleep duration and quality, with the arousal pathway identified as a key mediator alongside blue light.

sources.label: Exelmans L & Van den Bulck J. (2015). Bedtime mobile phone use and sleep in adults. Social Science & Medicine.
Hale L & Guan S. (2015). Screen time and sleep among school-aged children and adolescents: A systematic literature review. Sleep Medicine Reviews.

interventions.title: 3. Circadian Phase Delay
interventions.mechanism: Light exposure in the evening — including artificial light from screens — acts as a zeitgeber (time cue) that signals the body clock it is still daytime. This shifts the circadian phase later, pushing the natural sleep window into the night. Over time, this produces a pattern resembling mild social jetlag: the body's preferred sleep time drifts out of alignment with lifestyle demands, resulting in chronically shortened sleep and impaired sleep quality even when the total time in bed appears adequate.
interventions.evidence: Roenneberg et al. (2012) established in a large population study (n > 65,000) that artificial light exposure at night is a primary driver of social jetlag — the mismatch between biological and social clocks — which is independently associated with poorer health outcomes and reduced sleep quality. Wright et al. (2013) demonstrated that removing artificial light exposure (via a camping study) shifted circadian timing by nearly 2 hours within one week, directly earlier, confirming that evening artificial light — including screens — is a key modifiable driver of delayed sleep timing.

sources.label: Roenneberg T et al. (2012). Social jetlag and obesity. Current Biology.
Wright KP et al. (2013). Entrainment of the Human Circadian Clock to the Natural Light-Dark Cycle. Current Biology.

interventions.title: 4. Sleep Architecture Disruption
interventions.mechanism: Even when screen use does not prevent sleep onset, it can impair the internal structure of sleep itself. Melatonin suppression specifically reduces REM sleep in the first half of the night, and high pre-sleep arousal is associated with increased sleep fragmentation (more brief awakenings) and reduced slow-wave (deep) sleep. These effects degrade sleep quality independently of total sleep duration — a person can spend 8 hours in bed but wake feeling unrestored if their sleep architecture has been compromised.
interventions.evidence: Chang et al. (2015) found that screen readers experienced significantly less REM sleep and reported lower next-morning alertness than print readers, even after sleeping the same number of hours. A review by Cain and Gradisar (2010) across 36 studies found that electronic media use before bed was associated with increased sleep latency (time to fall asleep), reduced sleep duration, and crucially, subjective measures of unrestored sleep — consistent with architectural disruption rather than simply delayed onset. Gringras et al. (2015) specifically linked short-wavelength LED light to disrupted REM sleep timing in children and adults.

sources.label: Cain N & Gradisar M. (2010). Electronic media use and sleep in school-aged children and adolescents: A review. Sleep Medicine.
Gringras P et al. (2015). Bigger, Brighter, Bluer-Better? Current Light-Emitting Devices — Adverse Sleep Properties and Preventable Strategies. Frontiers in Public Health.

summaryTable.effect: Delayed sleep onset, reduced REM sleep
Longer time to fall asleep, fragmented sleep

summaryTable.mechanism: Evening light shifts body clock later
summaryTable.effect: Misaligned sleep timing, reduced total sleep
Less deep and REM sleep, unrestored waking

practicalNotes: Screen cutoff window: start with a 60-minute screen-free window before bed in weeks 1–2, extending to 90 minutes in weeks 3–6 to isolate the dose-response effect.
What counts as a screen: phones, tablets, laptops, and televisions all emit meaningful blue light — passive TV viewing is less disruptive than interactive device use, but still relevant.
Night mode / blue light filters: these reduce but do not eliminate the melatonin-suppressing effect (they do not address the arousal pathway at all). Treat them as partial mitigation, not a solution.

Sleep quality metrics to track: sleep latency (how long to fall asleep), number of night wakings, and morning restoration score are the most sensitive measures for this intervention — not just total sleep duration.
screen-sleep.note: The blue light and cognitive arousal pathways are largely independent — eliminating blue light (e.g. with blue-light glasses) without also addressing content engagement will only partially address the problem. A complete screen cutoff before bed tests both pathways simultaneously and is likely to produce the clearest signal across your 6-week exploration.

eating.docTitle: Does Time-Restricted Eating Improve My Energy Levels?
eating.docSubtitle: Evidence Summary for a 6-Week Personal Exploration
eating.summaryShort: Time-restricted eating aligns food intake with circadian metabolism, steadies blood glucose, supports overnight recovery, and may improve mitochondrial efficiency — without prescribing what you eat, only when.
eating.intro: Time-restricted eating (TRE) involves confining all food and caloric intake to a defined window — typically 8–10 hours — and fasting for the remainder of the 24-hour period. Unlike calorie-restriction diets, TRE does not prescribe what you eat, only when. Its effect on energy levels operates through four distinct but interconnected pathways.

interventions.title: 1. Circadian Metabolic Alignment
interventions.mechanism: The body has a master clock (the suprachiasmatic nucleus) and peripheral clocks in every metabolic organ — liver, gut, pancreas, adipose tissue. These clocks regulate when enzymes are produced, when insulin is most effective, and when fat oxidation peaks. Eating outside of daylight-aligned hours desynchronises these peripheral clocks from the central clock, impairing metabolic efficiency and producing the subjective experience of low energy and brain fog.
interventions.evidence: Panda et al.'s foundational work (2012, 2015) demonstrated in animal and human models that aligning food intake with the active phase of the circadian cycle improves metabolic markers independent of caloric intake. Chaix et al. (2019) reviewed this comprehensively, noting that even a modest reduction in eating window — from 15 hours to 10 hours — produced measurable improvements in circadian alignment and self-reported energy and sleep quality in shift workers and overweight adults.
interventions.practical: Starting your eating window within 1–2 hours of waking and closing it at least 3 hours before sleep aligns intake with peak metabolic and hormonal activity.

sources.label: Panda S. (2016). Circadian physiology of metabolism. Science.
Chaix A et al. (2019). Time-Restricted Eating to Prevent and Manage Chronic Metabolic Diseases. Annual Review of Nutrition.

interventions.title: 2. Blood Glucose Stability
interventions.mechanism: Energy crashes across the day are closely correlated with glycaemic variability — the degree to which blood glucose spikes and falls after meals. A longer daily fasting period improves insulin sensitivity, meaning cells respond more efficiently to glucose. This flattens the post-meal glucose curve, reducing the sharp dips that produce afternoon fatigue, irritability, and difficulty concentrating.
interventions.evidence: Sutton et al. (2018) conducted a randomised crossover trial in men with prediabetes and found that early TRE (eating window of approximately 6 hours, closing by 3pm) significantly improved insulin sensitivity, reduced blood pressure, and lowered oxidative stress — all without weight loss. This is notable because it isolates the timing effect from any caloric deficit. Wilkinson et al. (2020) replicated broadly similar findings in metabolic syndrome patients using a 10-hour window, with participants also reporting improved energy and reduced fatigue on validated questionnaires.

sources.label: Sutton EF et al. (2018). Early Time-Restricted Feeding Improves Insulin Sensitivity, Blood Pressure, and Oxidative Stress Even without Weight Loss in Men with Prediabetes. Cell Metabolism.
Wilkinson MJ et al. (2020). Ten-Hour Time-Restricted Eating Reduces Weight, Blood Pressure, and Atherogenic Lipids in Patients with Metabolic Syndrome. Cell Metabolism.

interventions.title: 3. Sleep Quality and Overnight Recovery
interventions.mechanism: Digestion is an energetically costly process. Eating close to bedtime forces the body to direct resources toward digestion during sleep, which elevates core body temperature, disrupts the natural drop in heart rate, and reduces slow-wave sleep — the most restorative sleep stage. Better sleep quality directly translates to higher baseline energy the following day and a shallower afternoon trough.
interventions.evidence: Lowe et al. (2020), in a 12-week randomised trial published in JAMA Internal Medicine, found that 16:8 TRE participants reported significantly improved sleep quality alongside other metabolic benefits. A separate study by Sutton et al. (2018) found that closing the eating window in the early afternoon correlated with measurably improved sleep architecture. The mechanism is supported by Roenneberg et al.'s extensive work on social jetlag — showing that metabolic and circadian misalignment consistently degrades sleep depth and duration.

sources.label: Lowe DA et al. (2020). Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters in Women and Men With Overweight and Obesity. JAMA Internal Medicine.
Roenneberg T et al. (2012). Social jetlag and obesity. Current Biology.

interventions.title: 4. Mitochondrial Efficiency and Cellular Energy Production
interventions.mechanism: During the fasting window, the body shifts from glucose as its primary fuel to fat oxidation and eventually mild ketone production. This metabolic switch improves mitochondrial efficiency — the organelles responsible for producing ATP (cellular energy). Periodic fasting also triggers mitophagy, a cellular clean-up process that removes damaged mitochondria and promotes the growth of new, more efficient ones. The net result is higher-quality energy production at the cellular level.
interventions.evidence: de Cabo and Mattson (2019) published a comprehensive review in the New England Journal of Medicine synthesising animal and human evidence for intermittent fasting (including TRE), finding robust evidence for improved mitochondrial efficiency and reduced oxidative stress. Moro et al. (2016) specifically studied TRE in resistance-trained males and found significant reductions in inflammatory markers and improvements in metabolic flexibility — the ability to efficiently switch between fuel sources — which is a key determinant of stable energy levels.

sources.label: de Cabo R & Mattson MP. (2019). Effects of Intermittent Fasting on Health, Aging, and Disease. New England Journal of Medicine.

Moro T et al. (2016). Effects of eight weeks of time-restricted feeding on basal metabolism, maximal strength, body composition, inflammation, and cardiovascular risk factors. Journal of Translational Medicine.

summaryTable.effect: More consistent energy across the day

practicalNotes: Window timing matters: earlier windows (e.g. 8am–6pm) show stronger metabolic effects than later ones (12pm–8pm), though the latter is more socially practical.
Adaptation period: energy may temporarily dip in weeks 1–2 as the body adjusts its fuel-switching machinery. This is normal and typically resolves by week 3.
Window consistency is key: irregular eating windows may undermine circadian benefits — try to open and close within 30 minutes of the same time daily.
eating.note: The strongest energy benefits from TRE appear to emerge from improved circadian alignment and blood glucose stability working together. For a clean 6-week experiment, hold window size and timing constant (e.g. 10-hour window, 7am–5pm or 8am–6pm) and track energy at consistent time points — mid-morning, post-lunch, and mid-afternoon — to capture where in the day the effect is most pronounced.
